The paper presents a methodology for reduced-order macromodels of multiport passive electromagnetic devices with embedded lumped elements.
Finite-element discretization of Maxwell’s curl equations is used for the spatial discretization.
Lumped resistors, capacitors, and inductors are directly incorporated into the state-space model.
The Krylov-subspace-based model-order reduction scheme is used to reduce the discrete state-space model.
The reduction method guarantees passivity if the original state-space model is passive.
The passivity of the original model is ensured by the properties of the matrices and the positivity of the lumped elements.
The method is validated on a terminated coaxial cable and a microstrip directional coupler.
The bandwidth of interest for the coaxial cable example is 600 MHz.
A reduced model of order 15 yields excellent accuracy across the entire bandwidth for the coaxial cable example.
The expansion frequency used for the coaxial cable example is 300 MHz.
The PRIMA model-order reduction process for a macromodel of order 20 requires 0.5 seconds per iteration for the coaxial cable example.
The accuracy of the reduced-order model is validated by comparing with the analytical solution of the transmission-line model.
Lumped elements are assigned along specific edges in the finite-element model.
The method assumes a linear electromagnetic system.
The incorporation of lumped inductors is done by adding a specific quantity to the matrix entry.
The discrete state-space model allows for direct incorporation of lumped elements.
The reduction method is compatible with general-purpose network analysis-oriented nonlinear simulation tools.
The method is applicable to both passive and active integrated planar circuits.
The use of lumped elements is justified by the small electrical size of the components.
The method is designed to support expedient design iteration and virtual prototyping.
The method is suitable for mixed-signal and mixed-physics integrated microsystems and nanosystems.
The method is applicable to three-dimensional multilayered geometries.
The method is compatible with broad-band multiport network representations.
The method is designed to facilitate and expedite finite-difference and finite-element modeling of structures with multiple instantiations of the same feature or subcomponent.
The method is suitable for the electromagnetic analysis of integrated microwave amplifiers.
